reasoning_notes:
Method. For each candidate I (a) mapped its link set onto the seven causal chains and asked whether the links sit on ONE chain or are scattered across several; (b) checked that first_seen_day is monotone along that chain's order; (c) required each link to rest on more than one independent source spread over several sites/regions; and (d) — decisive in many cases — went back to source_notes to check that the notes actually name the candidate entity with wording matching the claimed event, and that those notes come from different REGION-SITE-DEPT prefixes rather than one site echoing the same sentence.

What separated genuine from artefact.
1. Note-level corroboration. Many candidates have respectable aggregate statistics but no source note that names the entity for the claimed event (C-3, C-44, C-23, C-38, C-22, C-30, C-45, C-53, C-42, C-51, C-29, C-18, C-46). Their 'links' are background traffic about neighbouring entities (quarry-pay vs quarry-core, kestrel-pay vs kestrel-core, meridian427 vs meridian-pay455) that the aggregator attributed to the wrong asset. These rank lowest.
2. Echo vs independence. total_reports far exceeding independent_sources, with identical note text on a single day, is a broadcast, not corroboration. C-1 (tundra445: 'sensor readings drifting' repeated verbatim by ~10 teams on d061, 'nuisance trip' verbatim on d076) and C-39 (nimbusx532: five backlog notes all on d037, all from R06) are the clearest cases; C-52 (kestrel422, 14/18/7 reports on 4/10/3 sources) is the same pattern at lower intensity and I left it just outside the executive list.
3. One loud site. C-10 (nimbus-lite) and C-24 (quarry-pro597) have textbook policy_change -> ... -> regulatory_notice ordering, but nearly every corroborating note comes from R00S02 (different departments of one site). That is one compliance function's routine traffic, not a cross-organisational signal, so both sit below the cut despite clean ordering.
4. Scatter and disorder. C-16 (pellucid-pay456) has seven links spanning five unrelated chains — the archetypal artefact. C-9 (kestrel-pay) has six links on chain 1 but customer_escalation and component_defect both first appear on d001, before the supplier substitution that is supposed to cause them; C-4 has audit_finding after regulatory_notice; C-38 has forecast_revision before margin_compression; C-22 has checkout_drop before api_error_spike; C-43 has unplanned_downtime before sensor_drift. Out-of-order chains were pushed down regardless of volume.

The 18 I would put in front of an executive. C-26 (cobalt) and C-33 (arbor-na) are the strongest: five links each on chain 1, essentially perfect causal ordering, and notes naming the entity that hand the chain off between regions (arbor-na: defect in R04 d020 -> yield in R02 d030 -> shipment slip in R06 d057). C-28 (basalt-pay458) walks the whole firmware -> sensor_drift -> false_alarm -> downtime -> output_shortfall chain in order with R01 and R06 both reporting. C-8 (tundra-core) is the only complete pricing chain, with each stage named explicitly in notes and each stage owned by a different region (price R01 -> margin R03 -> discount R00 -> forecast R06). C-12, C-17, C-15, C-5, C-27, C-25 are attrition/backlog/SLA/penalty/churn progressions with multi-region note support; C-49, C-6, C-32 are the network -> latency -> batch -> reporting -> close chain (C-6 even has latency notes the link table omits); C-50 and C-55 are the compliance chain with genuinely distributed reporting, unlike C-10/C-24; C-35 and C-11 are supply chains with strong note support and only a minor ordering wobble (C-11 has yield at d008 two days before defect at d010); C-54 makes the list on the strength of its later stages even though its firmware_update link is concentrated in one site.

Just below the line (C-20, C-14, C-34, C-52, C-41, C-31) are plausible but each has one link resting on a single report, an unsupported root event, or heavy duplication. I set the executive list at 18 to keep precision high; extending to 24 would add these with a noticeable drop in confidence.
